title: Kingdom Theology
summary: The selected passages portray God’s reign through royal poetry, apocalyptic visions, Jesus’ announcement and parables, and Revelation’s proclamation. Psalm 2 pictures the nations resisting the Lord’s anointed king; Daniel 2 and 7 contrast earthly powers with a kingdom and dominion given by God; Matthew announces the kingdom and compares it to a small seed and leaven; Revelation 11 declares that the world’s kingdom belongs to God and his Messiah. The images differ, so the passages should not be collapsed into one description of how the kingdom arrives.
historical_context: The references move from a royal psalm and Daniel’s visions to sayings of Jesus and Revelation’s vision. These texts themselves provide the settings used here; the object’s sources do not establish a more specific reconstruction of the historical setting or the psalm’s original royal occasion.
canonical_context: Across these passages, divine rule is shown against rival human power. Psalm 2 uses royal language; Daniel’s visions depict kingdoms that rise and fall before God’s enduring authority; Jesus announces the kingdom and uses images of small beginnings and hidden growth; Revelation gives a climactic proclamation of God’s and the Messiah’s reign. These are related portrayals, not identical descriptions of timing or political form.
literary_context: The literary forms shape what each passage emphasizes. Psalm 2 is a royal poem; Daniel 2 and 7 use symbolic visions; Matthew 4 records a short proclamation and Matthew 13 a pair of parables; Revelation 11 gives a scene of heavenly acclamation. The royal claim, symbolic visions, parables, and proclamation each invite a different kind of reading.
covenantal_significance: Psalm 2 connects the king’s rule with the Lord’s purpose, while Daniel’s visions place human kingdoms under divine authority. Matthew presents Jesus announcing God’s kingdom and describing its growth with images that begin inconspicuously. Revelation 11 announces its final triumph. The sequence links kingship, divine sovereignty, Jesus’ teaching, and hope, while leaving the passages’ distinct imagery intact.
canonical_role: This entry brings together passages that portray divine rule in royal, visionary, teaching, and apocalyptic forms. Read together, they help readers notice both continuity in the theme of God’s reign and differences in how each text depicts it.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Kingdom Theology in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
